acquisition.why: Inbound channels work: Etsy/Shopify SEO, short-form video and paid ads. Agents can draft posts and listings, but filming production content needs a human. The market-stall channel in the source needs Ricardo in person, so drop it. Etsy dependence is a platform risk.

onboarding.why: The customer uploads photos and picks a pack size in a Shopify/Etsy personaliser. It is self-serve, with an occasional check of image resolution.

delivery.why: Physical goods, so delivery is capped. The source prints and presses by hand. Outsourcing to a UK print-on-demand supplier that makes magnets [E] could make it mostly hands-off, but at much lower margin.

billing.why: Shopify or Etsy checkout runs unattended.

support.why: Agents can handle 'where is my order' and reprint requests. Quality disputes and damaged items need a human decision.

scores.R_why: £300 covers a printer or print-on-demand samples, but 6-8 h/week with a toddler cannot cover hand-pressing or weekend markets. Using print-on-demand keeps it agent-run but likely cuts the 91% margin to roughly 30-50% [E]. UK demand exists, mainly as gifts.
scores.M_why: Photo magnets are heavily saturated on Etsy UK and Amazon, and Snapfish/Photobox sell them cheaply. The source's edge came from in-person markets and the founder's own content, and neither transfers to an agent-run setup.
scores.one_line: The revenue claims are strong but first-hand from a single video. The moat was in-person markets and manual craft, so an agent-run UK version becomes a low-margin print-on-demand Etsy shop in a crowded niche [E].

acquisition.why: It needs neighbourhood-by-neighbourhood density of consumers plus contractor recruitment. In practice that means leafleting, door-knocking and local groups, all human, and unsolicited DMs or SMS to consumers break PECR. Local paid ads (Nextdoor or Facebook) are possible but weak without density.

onboarding.why: Member sign-up can be a self-serve form. Vetting contractors (insurance, references, trade body membership) needs human checks.

delivery.why: Tradespeople do physical work on site. Scheduling batches, chasing no-shows and inspecting quality are all human coordination.

billing.why: Stripe handles membership fees. Collecting margin or commission from contractors needs reconciliation.

support.why: Complaints about home jobs (damage, poor work) carry consumer-law exposure and need human handling.

scores.R_why: Building local density and a contractor network needs time on the ground that he does not have. Bromley is viable demographically, but this is an ops-heavy local business, and Checkatrade/MyBuilder already serve the vetting need.
scores.M_why: The group-batching angle is mildly novel. However, UK incumbents (Checkatrade, Bark, MyBuilder, Nextdoor) dominate trade discovery, and margins between contractor and member are thin.
scores.one_line: This is a purely hypothetical pitch with no operator evidence. It needs local in-person density-building and contractor coordination, the opposite of an agent-run business.

acquisition.why: Amazon and Etsy search, paid social, and wholesale via Faire are inbound or marketplace-led, and agents can manage listings and ads. The business depends heavily on those platforms. Wholesale pitches to independent pet shops (mostly limited companies or sole traders) need care under PECR.

onboarding.why: Retail checkout is self-serve. Wholesale accounts arrive via Faire.

delivery.why: Physical inventory needs manufacturing, storage and shipping. Amazon FBA or a 3PL helps, but sourcing, quality control and restocking need humans. Bulky items hurt margins.

billing.why: Marketplace payouts run automatically. Wholesale invoicing is semi-automated.

support.why: Agents can handle returns and order questions within marketplace rules. Product safety complaints need a human.

scores.R_why: £300 barely covers a small print-on-demand range (bandanas) or samples. Real inventory needs much more capital. UK pet toys also carry product-safety duties, and margins after Amazon fees are tight.
scores.M_why: Pet accessories are a huge market but extremely crowded on Amazon UK and Etsy, with cheap Chinese competition. Differentiation needs branding and content.
scores.one_line: A vague 'six figures' second-hand claim. It is a viable market but capital-, inventory- and platform-heavy, with little edge for a £300 agent-run test.

acquisition.why: Buyers must come from an opt-in list built by content and SEO, which takes years to compound. Software vendors are mostly companies, so cold email to them is legal. The core asset (the audience) is the bottleneck.

onboarding.why: Agents can handle vendor intake forms and deal terms. Negotiating and vetting the software needs human judgement.

delivery.why: Curating deals and writing promotional emails suits agents well. Codes or affiliate links are fulfilled by the vendor.

billing.why: Affiliate networks or Stripe Connect handle the revenue share. Refund clawbacks need some reconciliation.

support.why: Buyer refund requests, broken lifetime deals and vendor disputes need human mediation.

scores.R_why: Without an existing audience, £300 and 6-8 h/week will not build a list big enough to monetise. He would compete as a tiny affiliate newsletter.
scores.M_why: AppSumo, PitchGround, Dealify and others dominate. Buyers are tired of lifetime deals, and AI tool-discovery newsletters are saturated.
scores.one_line: These are second-hand recollections about AppSumo, an established company with a pre-existing 50k list. It does not show a path for a newcomer without an audience in a saturated deals niche.

acquisition.why: Inbound only: OpenRent, SpareRoom, Airbnb monthly and contractor-housing platforms. Agents can manage listings and enquiries. It depends on these platforms.

onboarding.why: UK referencing, Right to Rent checks, deposits and licence or tenancy paperwork need human sign-off.

delivery.why: A physical property needs furnishing, cleaning between stays, repairs and inspections.

billing.why: Monthly rent collection via platform or standing order is automated. Arrears need a human.

support.why: Maintenance emergencies need contractors dispatched and human judgement.

scores.R_why: It needs a property purchase or a rent-to-rent lease. Both are far beyond £300. UK licensing (HMO, Renters' Rights Act changes) and Section 24 tax add further hurdles.
scores.M_why: There is real UK demand from NHS staff and contractors in London, but it is a capital-gated property play rather than a software one.
scores.one_line: There are no claims, despite a computed evidence score of 5. It is a capital-intensive property business that fails Ricardo's £300 test budget outright.

acquisition.why: Legal cold email only reaches limited companies. Many local trades are sole traders, who are off-limits under PECR. Closing a percentage-of-revenue deal usually needs a call. Content and ads to trades owners are a slow alternative.

onboarding.why: He must get the client's CRM or accounting export and verify a lawful basis or soft opt-in for each contact. That compliance check needs human judgement.

delivery.why: A GoHighLevel or Beehiiv workflow plus an AI copywriting agent can segment, send, auto-reply and book. A human approves the campaign and offer.

billing.why: A retainer is easy on Stripe. The revenue-share model needs the client's sales data, attribution and disputes, all handled by a human.

support.why: Agents can produce reporting and answer routine questions. Deliverability or complaint incidents need a human.

scores.R_why: His technical skills fit, and the tool cost fits £300. Barriers: PECR soft opt-in limits which past customers can be emailed, and SMS is riskier. Sales also need calls in limited hours. A small paid pilot with one or two limited-company clients is feasible [E].
scores.M_why: The GoHighLevel agency 'database reactivation' playbook is heavily saturated, and CRMs increasingly bundle AI reactivation features. Local UK firms are often sceptical of agencies.
scores.one_line: The first-hand claims are about Koerner's newsletter size, not service results, and client outcomes are hypothetical. Delivery automates well, but acquisition and consent checks keep humans involved.

acquisition.why: Showcase content, paid ads to professionals, and cold email to limited-company firms (brokers, course businesses) are legal. Closing retainers usually needs a call or demo.

onboarding.why: Agents can run the headshot and voice capture forms and the brief intake. Likeness and voice-clone consent, and financial-promotion compliance for brokers, need human review.

delivery.why: The HeyGen/ElevenLabs pipeline plus script-writing agents produce videos with little effort. A human does QA for 'AI tells' and for regulated claims.

billing.why: A Stripe subscription retainer runs unattended.

support.why: Agents can handle revision requests. Client approval loops and complaints about brand or accuracy need some human input.

scores.R_why: It is cheap to start (about £40-100/month in tools [E]) and remote, and suits a technical operator. FCA financial-promotion rules, ASA synthetic-media disclosure and consent add friction. Selling at about $1,500/month is ambitious in the UK [E].
scores.M_why: Clients can use HeyGen self-serve, so the agency layer is thin and commoditising fast. AI-video agencies are numerous, and buyers are increasingly wary of AI talking heads.
scores.one_line: Delivery is highly automatable and low-cost, but the service layer is being eaten by self-serve tools. Any edge must come from scripts and performance, and selling still takes calls.

acquisition.why: Direct-response paid social, Amazon or TikTok Shop and YouTube are inbound, and agents can iterate creatives. Ad spend needs are large, and the business depends on platforms.

delivery.why: A physical consumable needs formulation, manufacturing, CLP/detergent labelling compliance and fulfilment. All of that is human or supplier work.

billing.why: Checkout and marketplace payouts are automated.

support.why: Agents can handle routine order questions. Damage claims (fabric ruined, residue) need a human.

scores.R_why: Product development and stock, UK chemical safety and labelling rules (CLP, Detergents Regulations), and test ad budgets far exceed £300. Licensed characters are unrealistic.
scores.M_why: The cleaning category is dominated by big brands (Vanish, Dr. Beckmann) and cheap Amazon white-label products. Novel formats are possible but costly to validate.
scores.one_line: The evidence is a famous-brand anecdote (OxyClean) plus a speculative stain-sticker idea. It is a capital-, regulation- and ad-spend-heavy physical product unsuited to a £300 agent-run test.
